title: Full random walks with near-linear streaming space
formal:
Can a randomized graph-streaming algorithm sample a whole \(L\)-step random walk, for every \(1\le L\le n\), with total-variation error at most \(1/100\), near-linear bit space and polylogarithmically many passes?

More precisely, do there exist one uniform algorithm \(A\), constants \(C_s,C_p>0\) and fixed nonnegative integers \(a,b\) with the following property? For every unweighted directed graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), every start \(s\), every \(1\le L\le n\) and every fixed ordering of its edges, \(A\), knowing \(n,L,s\) before reading the stream, uses at most
\[C_s n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^a\text{ bits and }\left\lceil C_p\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b\right\rceil\text{ passes}\]
and outputs a tuple \((Y_0,\ldots,Y_L)\) whose distribution \(\nu_{G,s,L}\) satisfies
\[\|\nu_{G,s,L}-\mu_{G,s,L}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1/100?\]
Here \(\mu_{G,s,L}\) is the joint distribution of the ordinary directed random walk starting at \(s\), with the absorbing convention at a vertex of out-degree zero defined below.
why: Random-walk sampling is a basic graph primitive, and this question asks whether its full trajectory can be recovered with both modest memory and few sequential scans. It isolates a gap between known constant-pass tradeoffs and the possibility of polylogarithmically many passes.
status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 22, Kanpur 2009, with a 23 July 2021 update linking the two-pass result. The user selected a full trajectory for 1 <= L <= n, known start, unweighted directed graph and total-variation error at most 1/100. On 16 September 2026 the review checked the original 2011 reconstruction discussion, the 2021 full-version Theorems 1.1–1.3 and the published ITCS 2026 dense-graph result. Constant-pass lower bounds and the stronger unknown-start preprocessing lower bound do not exclude the selected polylogarithmic-pass algorithm; the dense-graph theorem assumes a minimum out-degree bound. A bounded later-work search found no verified resolution for the selected general-graph model. No new sampler, impossibility proof or Lean formalization is claimed.

progress.text: Das Sarma, Gollapudi and Panigrahy establish the near-linear-space, roughly square-root-in-\(L\) pass baseline and discuss full-walk reconstruction separately.
Chen and coauthors establish a two-pass space tradeoff and lower bounds for every fixed constant number of passes. Their full-trajectory and starting-vertex conventions are explicit.
Efremenko, Kol, Saxena and Zhang obtain one-pass sampling bounds exploiting a lower bound on every vertex out-degree. This advances dense-graph instances without settling arbitrary directed graphs.

importance.reason: A central streaming sampling problem linking sequential access, memory and long-range graph dependence. The known-start full-trajectory version preserves a substantive unresolved tradeoff beyond the established two-pass and dense-graph results.

sentences: The problem asks for one entire random-walk trajectory in a directed graph presented as an edge stream.
The start is known in advance, and the number of steps is at most the number of vertices.
The output distribution must be within 1/100 in total variation of the true joint distribution of all visits.
Near-linear bit space and a fixed polylogarithmic number of passes must suffice for every graph and edge order.
Known constant-pass tradeoffs and improved dense-graph samplers do not settle this general target.

definitions:
The graph has the known labeled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\), and edge set \(E\subseteq V\times V\). There are no multiple copies of an edge; self-loops are allowed. Both directions between distinct vertices may be present independently. Every edge has unit weight. The stream explicitly lists each directed edge once as a binary pair, in an arbitrary fixed order. Empty streams, isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and graphs with highly unequal degrees are allowed. The number of edges need not be known in advance.

For a vertex \(v\), its out-neighbor set is \(N^+(v)=\{w:(v,w)\in E\}\) and its out-degree is \(d^+(v)=|N^+(v)|\). A true random walk starts with \(X_0=s\). At every step, conditional on the complete history so far, if \(d^+(X_i)>0\), then \(X_{i+1}\) is chosen uniformly from \(N^+(X_i)\). New choices are independent conditional on the successive current vertices. Repeated visits and repeated traversal of an edge are permitted; this is not a simple path.

At a vertex of out-degree zero, define \(X_{i+1}=X_i\). This absorbing convention ensures that a length-\(L\) tuple is defined for every input. It is equivalent to adding a self-loop only at each zero-out-degree vertex. The convention is stated explicitly rather than leaving a uniform choice from an empty set undefined. It does not replace directed transitions elsewhere by undirected ones or add restarts from another vertex.

Equivalently, define the transition probabilities \(K_G(v,w)\) as \(1/d^+(v)\) when \(d^+(v)>0\) and \((v,w)\in E\), as one when \(d^+(v)=0\) and \(w=v\), and as zero otherwise. The desired law on \(V^{L+1}\) is
\[\mu_{G,s,L}(v_0,\ldots,v_L)=\mathbf1_{\{v_0=s\}}\prod_{i=0}^{L-1}K_G(v_i,v_{i+1}).\]
The integer \(L\) counts transitions, so the output lists \(L+1\) vertices including the start. The parameters \(n,L,s\) are explicitly available before the first pass. Only one sampled trajectory is requested.

For distributions \(\mu,\nu\) on this finite tuple space, total variation means
\[\|\nu-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{\omega\in V^{L+1}}|\nu(\omega)-\mu(\omega)|.\]
This compares the complete joint distributions, including dependencies between visits. Correct endpoint probabilities or correct single-time marginals alone do not establish the requirement. The output law averages over all internal random choices. The bound is not a probability that a numerical estimate is accurate, so a separate two-thirds-success convention is not substituted for it. Any probability assigned to an impossible trajectory is part of the total-variation error.

The algorithm returns an explicit tuple in \(V^{L+1}\), with initial vertex \(s\), after processing its passes. It must include every intermediate vertex, not just the endpoint, selected checkpoints, transition counts, a random seed or a program for reconstructing a longer object. The tuple may be assembled in working memory and then written to a final output tape. Its \(O(L\log(n+2))\) bits fit inside the allowed near-linear class because \(L\le n\); all working storage used to assemble it is counted.

A pass reads the full edge sequence from beginning to end. Between passes the algorithm may rewind and keep its working memory, but the sequence and its order remain the same. It cannot change the edge list, jump to an old edge, query an adjacency list or ask for a random neighbor except through computations on information acquired from the stream. There is no uncounted external scratch storage. This is an insertion-only arbitrary-order stream, not a randomly ordered or deletion stream.

Use one finite uniform randomized program for all parameter values. It may draw independent fair random bits. All mutable information counts toward bit space, including edge samples, labels, counters, retained randomness, intermediate structures and the assembled output. Old random choices can be reused only through information retained within that space. Pass and memory bounds hold on all executions. The algorithm must produce its tuple with probability one; no additional bound on local running time is imposed. The input graph and its edge ordering are fixed independently of the random choices.

The constants and logarithmic exponents in the statement do not depend on \(n,L,s,G\), its edge order or the random choices. Since \(L\le n\), a fixed polynomial in \(\log(n+2)\) and \(\log(L+2)\) is bounded by a fixed power of \(\log(n+2)\). Thus the displayed pass bound expresses the source's polylogarithmic target in the selected length range. In background bounds, \(\widetilde O\) and \(\widetilde\Omega\) hide fixed logarithmic factors; the target itself specifies their permitted form.

Knowing the start before reading the graph is important. A preprocessing summary that must later support any as-yet-unknown start has a stronger requirement. A lower bound for that stronger preprocessing task does not automatically apply to the present algorithm. Likewise, a theorem with a fixed constant pass count cannot be evaluated at a growing polylogarithmic pass count unless its uniform dependence on that parameter is proved.

The source asks broadly for faster simulation and separately for endpoint-distribution estimation and the most likely endpoints. With the user's approval, this card selects the full trajectory, fixed total-variation accuracy, unweighted directed input and length range \(1\le L\le n\). It retains the known-start and near-linear-space, polylogarithmic-pass objective.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying every condition above exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof that they do not. A positive answer must bound the total variation of the entire explicit output tuple and account for memory and passes on every graph and edge ordering. A negative answer must rule out all fixed logarithmic exponents \(a,b\) in the selected resource bounds, with the start known before streaming. Constant-pass lower bounds, lower bounds only for unknown-start preprocessing, endpoint-only samplers, results on dense graphs or bounds allowing a polynomial factor in \(L\) do not resolve this target. The tolerance \(1/100\) is the specified statistical distance between distributions, not an additive error on asymptotic resource bounds.

source_formulation.text: Panigrahy asks whether random-walk simulation can use near-linear space and only polylogarithmically many passes in the graph size and walk length. The source also asks separate questions about endpoint distributions. The user selected the entire trajectory of length at most n, a known initial vertex, unweighted directed graphs and total-variation error at most 1/100; the absorbing convention makes zero-out-degree inputs well defined.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase; user-approved trajectory output and length range

context_blocks.text: Random walks are useful for sampling and exploring large graphs, but a streaming algorithm encounters edges in an order unrelated to the trajectory it will eventually follow. Limited memory prevents retaining all possible future choices, while rereading the graph can be expensive.

A distribution on endpoints discards the route taken to reach them. Two samplers can agree at the endpoint while assigning very different probabilities to intermediate visits. The full-trajectory target therefore explicitly checks the joint law of all visited vertices.

Das Sarma, Gollapudi and Panigrahy obtain a near-linear-space simulation with roughly \(\sqrt L\) passes, up to logarithmic factors. Their basic procedure stores endpoints of walk segments; Remark 3.7 discusses reconstructing internal vertices, and §6 charges additional reconstruction space. The present output convention keeps that distinction visible.

Chen and coauthors give a two-pass sampler using \(\widetilde O(n\sqrt L\log(1/\delta))\) space and total-variation error \(\delta\). Choosing an inverse-polynomial \(\delta\le1/100\) meets the requested accuracy. For polynomially long walks, the extra factor \(\sqrt L\) can exceed every allowed logarithmic memory factor.

The same paper proves \(\widetilde\Omega(nL^{1/p})\) space lower bounds for each fixed pass count \(p\), with \(L=\lceil n^\beta\rceil\) and fixed \(\beta\in(0,1]\). These obstruct constant-pass near-linear-space simulation at such lengths, but do not rule out the growing polylogarithmic number of passes asked here. Its separate unknown-start result has a different quantifier order.

The 2026 dense-graph result gives much smaller one-pass memory when every vertex has sufficiently large out-degree. The minimum degree condition is essential to its guarantee; large average degree alone can leave a difficult region containing the chosen start. The result does not handle all directed graphs in the selected near-linear resource range.
